name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - General valence electronic configuration of p-block elements

questiontext.text: Which of the following represents the general valence shell electronic configuration of \(p\)-block elements (except helium)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(p\)-block elements, the last electron enters the outermost \(p\)-orbital. Since there are three \(p\)-orbitals, they can accommodate from \(1\) to \(6\) electrons.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Before the outermost \(p\)-orbitals begin filling, the outermost \(s\)-orbital is completely filled with \(2\) electrons (\(ns^2\)). Therefore, across Groups \(13\) to \(18\), the valence shell electronic configuration is \(ns^2np^{1\text{–}6}\) (except for helium, which has \(1s^2\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The general valence shell electronic configuration of \(p\)-block elements (except helium) is \(ns^2np^{1\text{–}6}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - Isotopic forms and natural abundance of boron

questiontext.text: Naturally occurring boron consists of two stable isotopes, \({}^{10}\mathrm{B}\) and \({}^{11}\mathrm{B}\). Their respective percentage abundances are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boron occurs in nature as a mixture of two isotopes of mass numbers \(10\) and \(11\), whose weighted average gives its atomic mass of \(10.81\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The natural isotopic abundances are \(19\%\) for \({}^{10}\mathrm{B}\) and \(81\%\) for \({}^{11}\mathrm{B}\). Checking the average: \(10 \times 0.19 + 11 \times 0.81 = 1.90 + 8.91 = 10.81\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The respective percentage abundances of \({}^{10}\mathrm{B}\) and \({}^{11}\mathrm{B}\) are \(19\%\) and \(81\%\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Abundance of aluminium in the Earth crust

questiontext.text: Which element is the most abundant metal and the third most abundant element by mass (\(8.3\%\)) in the Earth's crust?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The most abundant elements in the Earth's crust by mass are oxygen (\(45.5\%\)) and silicon (\(27.7\%\)), both of which are non-metals.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The third most abundant element overall—and the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust—is aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\)), with an abundance of \(8.3\%\) by mass.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aluminium is the most abundant metal and third most abundant element in the Earth's crust.

The most stable known isotope of nihonium has a half-life of \(20\text{ seconds}\).

The half-life of the most stable isotope of nihonium is \(20\text{ seconds}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Gallium low melting point and high boiling point

questiontext.text: Which Group \(13\) element has an unusually low melting point (\(303\text{ K}\)) so that it can exist in the liquid state during summer, yet has a high boiling point (\(2676\text{ K}\)) useful for measuring high temperatures?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While boron has a very high melting point (\(2453\text{ K}\)) due to its strong crystalline lattice, the heavier members of Group \(13\) are soft metals with low melting points.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga}\)) has a melting point of \(303\text{ K}\) (\(30^\circ\text{C}\)), which is close to warm summer temperatures, and a very high boiling point of \(2676\text{ K}\), giving it a wide liquid range suitable for high-temperature thermometry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The element is gallium.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Structural formula of borax

questiontext.text: Borax (\(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7\cdot 10H_2O}\)) actually contains tetranuclear \([\mathrm{B_4O_5(OH)_4}]^{2-}\) units. Its correct structural formula is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In crystalline borax, two of the ten water molecules are incorporated into the borate anion as four \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups, forming the tetranuclear \([\mathrm{B_4O_5(OH)_4}]^{2-}\) ion.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Subtracting \(2\mathrm{H_2O}\) from \(10\mathrm{H_2O}\) leaves \(8\mathrm{H_2O}\) molecules of crystallisation outside the coordination sphere, giving \(\mathrm{Na_2[B_4O_5(OH)_4]\cdot 8H_2O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct structural formula of borax is \(\mathrm{Na_2[B_4O_5(OH)_4]\cdot 8H_2O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Basic nature of aqueous borax solution

questiontext.text: An aqueous solution of borax is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Borax is the salt of a strong base (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) and a weak acid (orthoboric acid, \(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
In water, borax hydrolyses according to: \(\mathrm{Na_2B_4O_7 + 7H_2O \rightarrow 2NaOH + 4H_3BO_3}\). Because \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is a strong alkali and \(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\) is a weak acid, the resulting solution is basic (alkaline).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
An aqueous solution of borax is basic.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Reason for polymeric nature of boric acid

questiontext.text: Boric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)) has a polymeric layer structure due to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Individual \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\) molecules are planar triangular units that associate in the solid state into two-dimensional sheets.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Adjacent planar \(\mathrm{BO_3}\) units are linked together by intermolecular \(\mathrm{O-H\cdots O}\) hydrogen bonds, creating a polymeric layered structure.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Boric acid is polymeric due to the presence of hydrogen bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Hybridisation of boron in diborane

questiontext.text: The type of hybridisation of boron in diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)) is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each boron atom in \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) is surrounded by four hydrogen atoms (two terminal and two bridging) in a roughly tetrahedral arrangement.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
To form two terminal \(2c\text{-}2e\) bonds and two bridging \(3c\text{-}2e\) bonds, each boron atom uses four \(sp^3\) hybrid orbitals (three half-filled and one empty).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hybridisation of boron in diborane is \(sp^3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Thermodynamically most stable form of carbon

questiontext.text: Thermodynamically, the most stable allotropic form of carbon is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard enthalpy of formation (\(\Delta_f H^\circ\)) of the thermodynamically most stable allotrope of an element is taken as zero.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
For carbon, \(\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{graphite}) = 0\), whereas \(\Delta_f H^\circ(\text{diamond}) = +1.90\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta_f H^\circ(\mathrm{C_{60}}) = +38.1\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Graphite is thermodynamically the most stable form of carbon.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Common oxidation states of Group 14 elements

questiontext.text: Elements of Group \(14\) commonly:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Group \(14\) elements have four valence electrons (\(ns^2np^2\)). Because the sum of the first four ionisation enthalpies is very high, they generally form covalent compounds rather than simple \(\mathrm{M^{4+}}\) ions.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
These elements exhibit both the group oxidation state of \(+4\) (involving all four \(ns^2np^2\) electrons) and \(+2\) (involving only the \(np^2\) electrons, which becomes increasingly stable down the group).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Elements of Group \(14\) exhibit oxidation states of \(+2\) and \(+4\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Radioactive carbon isotope used in radiocarbon dating

questiontext.text: Which radioactive isotope of carbon, with a half-life of \(5770\text{ years}\), is used for radiocarbon dating?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Naturally occurring carbon has two stable isotopes (\({}^{12}\mathrm{C}\) and \({}^{13}\mathrm{C}\)) and a trace radioactive isotope.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The third isotope is \({}^{14}\mathrm{C}\), which is radioactive with a half-life of \(5770\text{ years}\) and is used for radiocarbon dating of archaeological samples.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The radioactive isotope used for radiocarbon dating is \({}^{14}\mathrm{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Maximum covalence of second-period p-block elements

questiontext.text: Boron forms only \([\mathrm{BF_4}]^-\) whereas aluminium forms \([\mathrm{AlF_6}]^{3-}\). This difference arises primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The maximum covalence of an element is limited by the number of available valence orbitals.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Boron belongs to the second period (\(n = 2\)), so its valence shell has only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals (four orbitals in total) and no \(d\)-orbitals. Therefore, its maximum covalence is restricted to \(4\), as in \([\mathrm{BF_4}]^-\). Aluminium belongs to the third period (\(3s^23p^1\)) and has vacant \(3d\)-orbitals lying between \(3p\) and \(4s\), allowing it to expand its covalence to \(6\) in \([\mathrm{AlF_6}]^{3-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The difference arises because boron lacks \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell whereas aluminium has vacant \(3d\)-orbitals.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Pi-bonding and coordination in nitrate vs phosphate

questiontext.text: In the \(+5\) oxidation state, nitrogen forms \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) (three-coordination) whereas phosphorus forms \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) (four-coordination). Which statement correctly explains the \(\pi\)-bonding in these oxoanions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Second-row \(p\)-block elements form strong \(p\pi\text{-}p\pi\) multiple bonds, whereas heavier \(p\)-block elements form \(\pi\)-bonds involving \(d\)-orbitals (\(d\pi\text{-}p\pi\) or \(d\pi\text{-}d\pi\)).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
In \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\), nitrogen has three-coordination and forms a \(p\pi\text{-}p\pi\) bond involving one nitrogen \(2p\)-orbital. In \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\), phosphorus has four-coordination and its \(\pi\)-bond involves \(s\), \(p\), and \(d\) orbitals (\(d\pi\text{-}p\pi\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) involves \(p\pi\text{-}p\pi\) bonding using a nitrogen \(p\)-orbital, whereas \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) involves \(s\), \(p\), and \(d\) orbitals contributing to the \(\pi\)-bond.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) involves a \(p\pi\text{-}p\pi\) bond using one nitrogen \(p\)-orbital, whereas \(\mathrm{PO_4^{3-}}\) involves \(s\), \(p\), and \(d\) orbitals contributing to the \(\pi\)-bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Atomic radius of gallium vs aluminium

questiontext.text: Although gallium (\(\mathrm{Ga}\)) lies below aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\)) in Group \(13\), the atomic radius of \(\mathrm{Ga}\) (\(135\text{ pm}\)) is smaller than that of \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(143\text{ pm}\)). Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atomic radius depends on the number of electron shells and the effective nuclear charge felt by the outermost electrons.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Aluminium has a noble-gas inner core (\([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^23p^1\)), whereas gallium has an inner core with \(10\) additional \(3d\)-electrons (\([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^24p^1\)). These \(10\) \(d\)-electrons offer poor screening effect for the outer electrons against the increased nuclear charge, pulling the valence shell closer to the nucleus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The smaller atomic radius of gallium is due to the poor shielding effect of the \(10\) inner \(d\)-electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Discontinuity in ionisation enthalpy in Group 13

questiontext.text: The ionisation enthalpy values in Group \(13\) do not decrease smoothly down the group; discontinuities are observed between \(\mathrm{Al}\) and \(\mathrm{Ga}\), and between \(\mathrm{In}\) and \(\mathrm{Tl}\). These discontinuities occur because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down a group, ionisation enthalpy normally decreases as atomic size increases, unless poorly shielding subshells (\(d\) or \(f\)) are filled.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Between \(\mathrm{Al}\) and \(\mathrm{Ga}\), \(10\) \(3d\)-electrons are added; between \(\mathrm{In}\) and \(\mathrm{Tl}\), \(14\) \(4f\)-electrons are added. Because \(d\)- and \(f\)-electrons have low screening effect, they cannot compensate for the increase in nuclear charge, causing \(\Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{Ga}) > \Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{Al})\) and \(\Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{Tl}) > \Delta_i H_1(\mathrm{In})\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The discontinuities are due to the inability of \(d\)- and \(f\)-electrons, which have low screening effect, to compensate for the increase in nuclear charge.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Electronegativity trend down Group 13

questiontext.text: How does the Pauling electronegativity vary on moving down Group \(13\) from boron (\(\mathrm{B}\)) to thallium (\(\mathrm{Tl}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electronegativity generally decreases down a group as atomic size increases, but size anomalies caused by poor \(d\)- and \(f\)-electron shielding alter this trend.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
From the Group \(13\) data, the Pauling electronegativity values are: \(\mathrm{B} = 2.0\), \(\mathrm{Al} = 1.5\), \(\mathrm{Ga} = 1.6\), \(\mathrm{In} = 1.7\), and \(\mathrm{Tl} = 1.8\). Thus, electronegativity first decreases from \(\mathrm{B}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}\) and then increases marginally from \(\mathrm{Al}\) to \(\mathrm{Tl}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Electronegativity first decreases from \(\mathrm{B}\) to \(\mathrm{Al}\) and then increases marginally down to \(\mathrm{Tl}\).

The sum is \(6887\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\), which prevents boron from forming \(\mathrm{B^{3+}}\) ions and forces it to form covalent compounds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Trend in Lewis acid strength of Group 13 trivalent compounds

questiontext.text: Trivalent compounds of Group \(13\) elements (such as \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) and \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\)) act as Lewis acids. How does the tendency to behave as a Lewis acid change down Group \(13\)?

generalfeedback.text:

In trivalent Group \(13\) compounds (\(\mathrm{EX_3}\)), the central atom has only six electrons in its valence shell (electron-deficient) and tends to accept an electron pair to complete its octet.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
As the atomic size of the central atom increases down Group \(13\) from \(\mathrm{B}\) to \(\mathrm{Tl}\), the attraction for an incoming lone pair decreases. Therefore, the tendency to behave as a Lewis acid decreases down the group.

The tendency to behave as a Lewis acid decreases with the increase in size down the group.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - White fumes around anhydrous aluminium chloride bottle

questiontext.text: White fumes appear around a bottle of anhydrous aluminium chloride (\(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\)) when opened in moist air. This is due to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is covalent and strongly hygroscopic, undergoing partial hydrolysis upon contact with atmospheric moisture.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Reaction of anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) with atmospheric water vapour liberates \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas. Moist \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas condenses with water vapour in the air to appear as white fumes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
White fumes appear because anhydrous \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is partially hydrolysed by atmospheric moisture to liberate \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Species formed by AlCl3 in acidified aqueous solution

questiontext.text: In an acidified aqueous solution, aluminium chloride forms a complex ion. Identify the complex ion and the hybridisation state of \(\mathrm{Al}\) in it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In acidified aqueous solution, \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) coordinates six water molecules using its vacant \(3s\), \(3p\), and \(3d\) orbitals.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The complex ion formed is the octahedral hexaaquaaluminium(III) ion, \([\mathrm{Al(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}\). Since six electron pairs from six \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) ligands are accepted into one \(3s\), three \(3p\), and two \(3d\) orbitals of \(\mathrm{Al}\), the hybridisation state of \(\mathrm{Al}\) is \(sp^3d^2\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The complex ion is \([\mathrm{Al(H_2O)_6}]^{3+}\) and the hybridisation state of \(\mathrm{Al}\) is \(sp^3d^2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Transport of concentrated nitric acid in aluminium containers

questiontext.text: Concentrated nitric acid (\(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)) can be safely transported in aluminium containers because:

Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Although aluminium is an amphoteric metal that dissolves in dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and aqueous alkalies, it behaves differently toward strong oxidising acids.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) is a strong oxidising agent that forms a very thin, impervious protective layer of aluminium oxide (\(\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)) on the metal surface, rendering aluminium passive toward further reaction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) renders aluminium passive by forming a protective oxide layer on its surface.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Reaction of aluminium with aqueous sodium hydroxide

questiontext.text: When aluminium metal reacts with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), it dissolves to form a soluble complex salt and liberates a gas. Identify the complex salt and the gas:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aluminium is amphoteric in nature and reacts with both mineral acids and aqueous alkalies.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The balanced equation for the reaction of aluminium with aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) is:
\[2\mathrm{Al(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^-(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)}\]
Thus, the soluble complex salt is sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate(III), \(\mathrm{Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^-}\), and the gas liberated is dihydrogen (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products are \(\mathrm{Na^+[Al(OH)_4]^-}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Non-existence of thallium triiodide among Group 13 trihalides

questiontext.text: Group \(13\) elements react with halogens to form trihalides of the general formula \(\mathrm{EX_3}\) (\(\mathrm{X = F, Cl, Br, I}\)), with the exception of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In thallium, the \(+1\) oxidation state is far more stable than the \(+3\) oxidation state due to the inert pair effect, making \(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}}\) a strong oxidising agent.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
While \(\mathrm{BF_3}\), \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), \(\mathrm{GaBr_3}\), and \(\mathrm{InI_3}\) exist as trihalides, \(\mathrm{TlI_3}\) does not exist as a stable thallium(III) iodide (in fact, \(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}}\) oxidises \(\mathrm{I^-}\) to \(\mathrm{I_3^-}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The exception among Group \(13\) trihalides is \(\mathrm{TlI_3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Standard electrode potentials and stability of Al3+ vs Tl3+

questiontext.text: Given \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al}) = -1.66\text{ V}\) and \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}/Tl}) = +1.26\text{ V}\), which conclusion is valid regarding their behaviour in aqueous solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A large negative standard reduction potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M^{3+}/M})\) indicates a strong tendency for the metal to be oxidised to \(\mathrm{M^{3+}(aq)}\), whereas a large positive \(E^\circ\) indicates that \(\mathrm{M^{3+}}\) is unstable and acts as a strong oxidising agent.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al}) = -1.66\text{ V}\), aluminium readily forms \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}(aq)}\) and is strongly electropositive. Since \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}/Tl}) = +1.26\text{ V}\), \(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}}\) is unstable in solution and is a powerful oxidising agent; \(\mathrm{Tl^+}\) is more stable in solution than \(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aluminium is more electropositive than thallium, and \(\mathrm{Tl^{3+}}\) is unstable in aqueous solution and acts as a powerful oxidising agent.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Reaction of orthoboric acid with water as Lewis acid

questiontext.text: Which equation correctly represents the acidic behaviour of orthoboric acid (\(\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\)) in water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Orthoboric acid is not a protonic acid; it does not release \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions on its own. Instead, it acts as a weak monobasic Lewis acid.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The electron-deficient boron atom accepts a pair of electrons from a hydroxyl ion (\(\mathrm{OH^-}\)) of a water molecule to complete its octet, releasing \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) in solution:
\[\mathrm{B(OH)_3 + 2H_2O \rightarrow [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+}\].

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct equation is \(\mathrm{B(OH)_3 + 2H_2O \rightarrow [B(OH)_4]^- + H_3O^+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Preparation of diborane using LiAlH4 in diethyl ether

questiontext.text: In the preparation of diborane by treating boron trifluoride with \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) in diethyl ether, what are the stoichiometric coefficients of \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) and \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) to produce \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)?

Step 1: Given Data and Conditions

Balancing boron: \(2\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) require \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{BF_3}\). Hydrogen check: \(3 \times 4 = 12\) on left, \(2 \times 6 = 12\) on right. Thus, \(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) and \(3\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{LiAlH_4}\) are required.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q32 - Covalent radius trend in Group 14 elements

From \(\mathrm{Si}\) to \(\mathrm{Pb}\), completely filled \(d\)- and \(f\)-orbitals are present in the inner core, whose poor shielding increases effective nuclear charge and limits further expansion in radius.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The small increase from \(\mathrm{Si}\) to \(\mathrm{Pb}\) is due to the presence of completely filled \(d\)- and \(f\)-orbitals in heavier members.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q36 - Why heavier Group 14 elements do not form p-pi p-pi bonds

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q40 - Hybridisation, shape and C-O bond length in carbon dioxide

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q49 - Electron deficiency of BCl3 vs electron-precise SiCl4

questiontext.text: Compare \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) and \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\) with respect to electron deficiency:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An electron-deficient molecule is one in which the central atom has fewer than \(8\) electrons in its valence shell.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
In \(\mathrm{BCl_3}\), boron has \(3 + 3 = 6\) valence electrons around it, so it is electron-deficient and acts as a Lewis acid. In \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\), silicon has \(4 + 4 = 8\) valence electrons around it, so it is an electron-precise molecule (not electron-deficient), even though it can accept lone pairs from donors like \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) using its vacant \(3d\)-orbitals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{BCl_3}\) is an electron-deficient species (\(6\) valence electrons on \(\mathrm{B}\)), whereas \(\mathrm{SiCl_4}\) is an electron-precise species (\(8\) valence electrons on \(\mathrm{Si}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q50 - Phenomenal decrease in ionisation enthalpy from carbon to silicon

questiontext.text: The first ionisation enthalpy drops sharply from carbon (\(1086\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)) to silicon (\(786\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)), whereas from \(\mathrm{Si}\) to \(\mathrm{Pb}\) the change is much smaller. The sharp drop from \(\mathrm{C}\) to \(\mathrm{Si}\) is caused by:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
First ionisation enthalpy decreases sharply when valence electrons move to a higher principal shell with effective inner-shell screening and a large jump in atomic size.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Moving from \(\mathrm{C}\) (\(77\text{ pm}\)) to \(\mathrm{Si}\) (\(118\text{ pm}\)), the covalent radius increases substantially and the valence \(3p\) electrons are shielded by a complete \(2s^22p^6\) core. This greatly reduces nuclear attraction on the outermost electron, causing \(\Delta_i H_1\) to drop by \(300\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The sharp decrease from \(\mathrm{C}\) to \(\mathrm{Si}\) is due to the large increase in atomic size and the increased screening effect of the inner \(2s^22p^6\) shell.

answer.text: a large increase in atomic size and increased screening by the inner \(2s^22p^6\) shell

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q51 - Thermal instability of PbCl4 and stability of PbCl2

questiontext.text: Lead(IV) chloride (\(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\)) is highly unstable towards heat and decomposes readily on warming into:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In lead, the \(+2\) oxidation state is much more stable than the \(+4\) oxidation state due to the inert pair effect.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Upon heating, \(\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}\) in \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) oxidises \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) to \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) and gets reduced to stable \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\):
\[\mathrm{PbCl_4(l) \xrightarrow{\Delta} PbCl_2(s) + Cl_2(g)}\]

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) decomposes on heating to \(\mathrm{PbCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q52 - Reason lead does not form PbI4

questiontext.text: Lead is known not to form an iodide, \(\mathrm{PbI_4}\), because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To form a tetravalent halide \(\mathrm{PbX_4}\), lead must unpair its \(6s^2\) electrons and promote one electron to a \(6p\)-orbital, which requires promotion energy compensated by bond formation.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
The \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bond initially formed during the reaction is weak and does not release enough energy to unpair the \(6s^2\) electrons and excite one of them to a higher orbital to provide four unpaired electrons around the lead atom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{PbI_4}\) does not exist because \(\mathrm{Pb-I}\) bond formation does not release sufficient energy to unpair and excite the \(6s^2\) electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q53 - Why SiF6 2- exists whereas SiCl6 2- does not

questiontext.text: \([\mathrm{SiF_6}]^{2-}\) is well known, whereas \([\mathrm{SiCl_6}]^{2-}\) is not. Which pair of reasons explains this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stability of a \(6\)-coordinated complex ion \([\mathrm{SiX_6}]^{2-}\) requires both steric accommodation of six ligands around \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) and strong donor–acceptor orbital interaction.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
First, six large \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions cannot be accommodated around the small \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) ion due to size limitations (steric crowding). Second, the interaction between the lone pair of a chloride ion and \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) is not very strong compared to that of \(\mathrm{F^-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Six large \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions cannot fit around small \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\), and the \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\)–\(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) lone-pair interaction is weak.

answer.text: Six large \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) ions cannot be accommodated around small \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\), and the interaction between the lone pair of \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\) and \(\mathrm{Si^{4+}}\) is weak.
Silicon lacks \(3d\)-orbitals for chlorine, whereas it uses \(3d\)-orbitals for fluorine.
Chlorine is more electronegative than fluorine, so it cannot donate a lone pair.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q54 - Heat released during combustion of diborane

questiontext.text:
Diborane burns spontaneously in oxygen according to the equation:
\[\mathrm{B_2H_6(g) + 3O_2(g) \rightarrow B_2O_3(s) + 3H_2O(l)};\quad \Delta_r H^\circ = -1976\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
How much heat is released when \(14\text{ g}\) of diborane (molar mass \(\approx 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\)) undergoes complete combustion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Mass of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6} = 14\text{ g}\); molar mass of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6} = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\); \(\Delta_r H^\circ = -1976\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Number of moles \(n = \frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molar mass}}\); Heat released \(q = n \times |\Delta_r H^\circ|\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
\[n = \frac{14\text{ g}}{28\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.5\text{ mol}\]
\[q = 0.5\text{ mol} \times 1976\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} = 988\text{ kJ}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(0.5\text{ mol}\) is half of \(1\text{ mol}\), so half of \(1976\text{ kJ}\) is \(988\text{ kJ}\). Thus, \(988\text{ kJ}\) of heat is released.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q56 - Moles of carbon in a three-carat diamond

questiontext.text: Diamond is measured in carats, where \(1\text{ carat} = 200\text{ mg}\). How many moles of carbon atoms are present in a \(3\text{-carat}\) diamond (atomic mass of \(\mathrm{C} = 12\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
\(1\text{ carat} = 200\text{ mg}\); mass of diamond \(= 3\text{ carats}\); atomic mass of carbon \(= 12\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\text{Moles} = \frac{\text{Mass in grams}}{\text{Molar mass in g mol}^{-1}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Total mass \(= 3 \times 200\text{ mg} = 600\text{ mg} = 0.600\text{ g}\).
\[\text{Moles of C} = \frac{0.600\text{ g}}{12\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.05\text{ mol}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(0.05\text{ mol} \times 12\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 0.6\text{ g} = 600\text{ mg} = 3\text{ carats}\). Thus, \(0.05\text{ mol}\) of carbon atoms are present.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q57 - Chemical reactions of silicon dioxide with HF and NaOH

questiontext.text: Silica (\(\mathrm{SiO_2}\)) resists attack by halogens, dihydrogen, and most acids, but reacts with \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\). What are the silicon-containing products formed in these two reactions, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Despite its high \(\mathrm{Si-O}\) bond enthalpy, \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) is an acidic oxide that reacts with strong bases like \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) and with \(\mathrm{HF}\) (forming volatile \(\mathrm{SiF_4}\)).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
With \(\mathrm{HF}\): \(\mathrm{SiO_2 + 4HF \rightarrow SiF_4 + 2H_2O}\).
With \(\mathrm{NaOH}\): \(\mathrm{SiO_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SiO_3 + H_2O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The silicon-containing products are \(\mathrm{SiF_4}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2SiO_3}\), respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q58 - Silicone polymer structure formed from RSiCl3

questiontext.text: If \(\mathrm{RSiCl_3}\) is used as the starting material for the manufacture of silicones (via hydrolysis followed by condensation polymerisation), the resulting polymer will be a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The dimensionality of a silicone polymer is governed by the number of hydrolysable \(\mathrm{Cl}\) atoms on the starting chlorosilane.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{RSiCl_3}\) yields \(\mathrm{RSi(OH)_3}\), which has three \(\mathrm{-OH}\) groups per silicon atom. Condensation polymerisation therefore proceeds in three directions, forming a complex three-dimensional cross-linked silicone polymer.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Using \(\mathrm{RSiCl_3}\) produces a three-dimensional cross-linked silicone polymer.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q59 - Charge generation in aluminosilicates like zeolites

questiontext.text: When a few silicon atoms in the three-dimensional network of \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) are replaced by aluminium atoms to form an aluminosilicate (such as feldspar or zeolites), the overall framework acquires:

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The aluminosilicate framework acquires a negative charge balanced by cations such as \(\mathrm{Na^+}\), \(\mathrm{K^+}\), or \(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q60 - Bonding and donor site in carbon monoxide

Between carbon and oxygen there is one \(\sigma\)-bond and two \(\pi\)-bonds (a triple bond). Because of the lone pair on the carbon atom, \(\mathrm{CO}\) acts as a donor ligand and reacts with certain metals on heating to form metal carbonyls.

\(\mathrm{CO}\) contains one \(\sigma\)-bond and two \(\pi\)-bonds, with a lone pair on carbon acting as a donor to form metal carbonyls.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_P_BLOCK_ELEMENTS_MCQ_Q61 - Stoichiometry of hydrogen gas evolved in borazine synthesis

questiontext.text: When diborane reacts with ammonia and the resulting adduct is heated to form borazine (\(\mathrm{B_3N_3H_6}\)), how many moles of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas are liberated per mole of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) consumed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reactants: \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) and \(\mathrm{NH_3}\); products: borazine (\(\mathrm{B_3N_3H_6}\)) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The balanced equation for the thermal conversion is:
\[3\mathrm{B_2H_6 + 6NH_3 \rightarrow 3[BH_2(NH_3)_2]^+[BH_4]^- \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2B_3N_3H_6 + 12H_2}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
From the balanced equation, \(3\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) produce \(12\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\). Therefore, \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) produces:
\[\frac{12}{3} = 4\text{ mol of }\mathrm{H_2}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
\(4\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas are liberated per mole of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) consumed.
